blocks.text: 1. API Ingestion
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708805-151917111.png
API Ingestion, covering a structured source with its own real time characteristics, shifts focus from directly queried databases to externally hosted services.
It pulls records out of an external service's API into the document collection.
2. Recapping The Preview
Database Ingestion's closing recap previewed API ingestion as a structured source with its own real time characteristics, briefly described there.
This topic gives that preview its complete, dedicated treatment, exploring every detail only briefly hinted at before.
3. Databases Versus APIs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708806-241413697.png
Database Ingestion covered reaching a database directly. An API instead sits in front, controlling access.
That control layer changes how ingestion has to behave.

blocks.text: 4. Authentication And Rate Limits
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708806-564209049.png
Most APIs require credentials, and enforce a maximum request rate.
Ingestion code has to respect both, or risk being blocked entirely.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Ignoring a rate limit does not just slow ingestion down. Many APIs revoke access entirely after repeated violations, turning a minor pacing mistake into a blocked integration.

blocks.text: 5. Pagination Across Responses
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708807-81203905.png
Large result sets arrive split across multiple pages, not one single response.
Ingestion code has to walk through every page before the full dataset is complete.
6. JSON Response Structure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708807-276537270.png
Most APIs return JSON, a nested, structured format.
Turning that nested JSON into flat, readable text is the same underlying challenge as converting rows to natural language, covered generally in Database Ingestion.
7. Polling Versus Webhooks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708807-429888634.png
Polling repeatedly asks the API if anything is new; webhooks instead push updates automatically.
This mirrors keeping ingested data synchronized, covered generally in Database Ingestion: two different ways to stay current.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Synchronization method","How it stays current"],"rows":[["Polling","Repeatedly asks the API if anything changed"],["Webhooks","The API pushes updates automatically as they happen"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Handling Partial Failures
A single failed request should not silently drop that batch of records forever.
Retrying or logging the failure keeps ingestion reliable over time.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A well designed API ingestion pipeline tracks which pages or records it has already successfully pulled, so a retry after a failure resumes from where it left off instead of starting over.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When API Ingestion Is The Right Ingestion Source

blocks.alt: Recognizing When API Ingestion Is The Right Ingestion Source
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446708808-564359632.png
API ingestion suits live, externally hosted services reached over a network.
Database ingestion, covered generally in Database Ingestion, remains preferable for already local, internal tables.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Firing requests as fast as possible without respecting the API's documented rate limit.
Reading only the first page of results and silently missing everything beyond it.
Feeding raw, nested JSON directly into the pipeline without flattening it into readable text.
Treating a failed request as a reason to abandon the entire ingestion run instead of retrying just that page.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: API ingestion pulls records out of an external service's API into the document collection.
Unlike a direct database connection, an API sits in front, controlling access.
Most APIs require credentials and enforce a maximum request rate that ingestion code must respect.
Large result sets arrive split across multiple pages, requiring the pipeline to walk through all of them.
Most APIs return nested JSON, which needs flattening into readable text before it becomes a document.
Polling repeatedly asks for updates; webhooks instead push updates automatically.
A single failed request should be retried or logged, not allowed to silently drop data.
API ingestion suits live, externally hosted services; database ingestion suits already local tables.
